d: Availability percentages, SLAs, and how much downtime each nine allows
goal: Your win today: you can turn '99.9%' into 'about 9 hours of downtime a year, 43 minutes a month', explain what an SLA is, and say why chaining services lowers availability.
bookSections: 'Availability numbers' (high availability definition, SLA, cloud provider SLAs, Table 2-3 nines and downtime)

stages.title: What a nine buys you
stages.teaches: High availability = the ability of a system to stay continuously operational for a desirably long period. It's measured as a percentage of time up: 100% means never down; most services sit between 99% and 100%. An SLA (service level agreement) is an agreement between a service provider and its customer that formally defines the uptime the service will deliver. Amazon, Google and Microsoft set their cloud SLAs at 99.9% or above. Uptime is traditionally counted in nines; more nines = less downtime. Table 2-3: 99% → 14.40 min/day, 1.68 h/week, 7.31 h/month, 3.65 days/year. 99.9% → 1.44 min/day, 10.08 min/week, 43.83 min/month, 8.77 h/year. 99.99% → 8.64 s/day, 1.01 min/week, 4.38 min/month, 52.60 min/year. 99.999% → 864 ms/day, 6.05 s/week, 26.30 s/month, 5.26 min/year. 99.9999% → 86.40 ms/day, 604.80 ms/week, 2.63 s/month, 31.56 s/year.
stages.interaction: Predict first: '99.9% uptime allows how much downtime per year?' options: '8.77 hours' / '3.65 days' / '52 minutes'. Then the Nines Dial: a big rotary selector with 2 to 6 nines. Under it, a year strip of 365 small day-cells; the allowed downtime is drawn as a red block (at 99% it covers ~3.65 day-cells; at 99.9% a sliver of one cell; beyond that a magnifier pops out showing minutes/seconds). Four readouts (per day / week / month / year) count up to the Table 2-3 values each time the dial turns. A side caption updates: '2 nines: a bad weekend', '3 nines: one long evening a year', '5 nines: a coffee break a year'.
stages.check: Prediction scored (correct: 8.77 hours). Q.quiz: 'A cloud SLA promises 99.99%. About how much downtime is that per month?' options: 'About 4.4 minutes' (correct) / 'About 44 minutes' / 'About 26 seconds'.

stages.title: Do the math yourself
stages.teaches: Formula: allowed downtime = (100% − availability) × period. The book's table uses a 365.25-day year (8,766 hours, 525,960 minutes) and a month of 1/12 of that (~30.44 days, ~43,830 minutes). Shortcut: every extra nine divides downtime by 10 (8.77 h → 52.6 min → 5.26 min → 31.6 s per year). Odd targets like 99.95% sit halfway in log terms: 0.05% × 43,830 min ≈ 21.9 min/month.
stages.interaction: Calculate-and-check, 4 cards. Each shows availability + period, a formula strip '(1 − A) × period' with the learner filling in the number and choosing a unit (s / min / h / days). Cards: (1) 99.9% per month → 43.8 min; (2) 99.99% per year → 52.6 min; (3) 99.95% per month → 21.9 min; (4) 99.5% per year → 43.8 h (1.83 days accepted). Tolerance ±10% and any equivalent unit. On a miss, show the worked line and a 'divide by 10 per nine' staircase graphic linking it to the table.
stages.check: Q.quiz: 'Going from 99.9% to 99.99% changes yearly downtime from 8.77 hours to…' options: 'about 52.6 minutes, ten times less' (correct) / 'about 4.4 hours, half as much' / 'about 5.3 minutes, a hundred times less'.

stages.title: Chains and spares
stages.teaches: Beyond the book, but interviewers ask it. Series: if a request needs services A AND B AND C, overall availability = A × B × C. Three services at 99.9% each → 0.999³ ≈ 99.7% (≈ 26 hours down a year, three times worse than any one of them). Parallel: if any one of two independent replicas can serve, availability = 1 − (1 − A)². Two 99% boxes → 1 − 0.01² = 99.99%. So redundancy is how you buy nines; long dependency chains are how you lose them. Big caveat: the parallel formula assumes failures are independent. Replicas in the same rack, same region, or running the same bad deploy fail together, so real gains are smaller.
stages.interaction: A drag-and-wire sandbox. Palette of blocks: 'Server 99%', 'Service 99.9%', 'Service 99.99%'. Learner drops blocks between a 'User' node and a 'Done' node, either in a row (series) or stacked (parallel group). A live readout shows overall availability and downtime/year, recomputed on every change, with the formula shown under the readout. Three challenges unlock in turn (no locks; just suggested order): (1) 'Chain three 99.9% services. What do you get?' → ~99.7%; (2) 'Reach at least 99.99% using only 99% servers' → two in parallel; (3) 'Your API (99.99%) depends on a 99.9% database. Fix it to reach at least 99.95% end to end' → add a parallel database replica. Then a 'correlated failure' toggle puts both replicas in one rack; a lightning bolt hits the rack and both die, and the readout shows a warning that the formula assumed independence.
stages.check: Q.quiz: 'Your feature calls 4 services, each 99.9% available, one after another. Best estimate of end-to-end availability?' options: 'About 99.6%' (correct) / '99.9%, same as each one' / '99.9999%, because there are four of them'.

stages.title: Read the fine print
stages.sub: SLA vs SLO vs SLI, and what an SLA really promises
stages.teaches: The book defines SLA only; the Google SRE book adds two terms you'll hear in senior conversations. SLI (service level indicator) = a measured number, e.g. 'fraction of requests that succeeded in the last 30 days'. SLO (service level objective) = the internal target for that number, e.g. '99.9% of requests succeed'. SLA = the external contract with consequences if missed; cloud SLAs typically pay service credits (a partial refund), they don't guarantee uptime. Teams set the SLO tighter than the SLA so they notice trouble before it costs money. Error budget = 1 − SLO: at 99.9%, about 43 minutes a month of failure you can 'spend' on risky deploys. Exact provider SLA numbers differ per product and change over time; check the current pages (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure are the book's references).
stages.interaction: Sort-into-buckets: 8 statement cards to drop into SLI / SLO / SLA bins. Examples: 'p99 latency measured over 28 days' → SLI; 'We aim for 99.9% of requests to succeed' → SLO; 'If monthly uptime is below 99.99% you get a 10% credit' → SLA; 'Fraction of health checks that passed' → SLI; 'Internal target: 99.95% availability' → SLO; 'Contract with the customer, with refunds if missed' → SLA; 'Error rate over the last hour' → SLI; 'Alert us when we're burning our monthly budget too fast' → SLO. Then an error-budget meter: a month bar with 43.8 minutes of budget (99.9%); the learner clicks 'deploy' events (each costs a random 2–8 minutes of errors) and watches the budget drain, with a note at zero: 'freeze risky launches until the budget recovers'.
stages.check: Q.quiz: 'A cloud provider misses its 99.99% SLA one month. What usually happens?' options: 'Customers can claim service credits, a partial refund' (correct) / 'The provider must pay for all customer losses' / 'Nothing, because the SLA is only an internal goal'.

stages.title: Boss: The Nines Merchant
stages.teaches: Applies the quest: more nines cost more (redundancy, multi-region, on-call). Pick a target that matches the cost of being down.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with per-scenario choices (the engine supports scenario.choices). (1) 'Product wants 99.999% for an internal monthly reporting dashboard.' choices: 'Overkill: 99.9% or less is fine; 5 nines means about 5 minutes a year and costs a lot' (correct) / 'Right target' / 'Too low, aim for 6 nines'. (2) 'Your service calls 5 dependencies at 99.9% each and you promised customers 99.9%.' choices: 'Can't hold it: chained you're near 99.5%, so add redundancy or remove hard dependencies' (correct) / 'Fine, every dependency meets 99.9%' / 'Fine if you add more servers in a row'. (3) 'Two replicas of a 99% service, same rack, same power supply. Claimed availability: 99.99%.' choices: 'Optimistic: shared rack means correlated failures' (correct) / 'Correct, 1 − 0.01²' / 'Too pessimistic'. (4) 'Engineer: 99.9% means we can be down 8.77 hours a month.' choices: 'Wrong: that's per year; per month it's about 43.8 minutes' (correct) / 'Right' / 'Wrong: it's 8.77 minutes a month'. (5) 'A payments API runs at 99%.' choices: 'Too low: that's 3.65 days of failed payments a year' (correct) / 'Right target' / 'Overkill'.
stages.check: Boss HP; each 'why' links back to Table 2-3 or the series/parallel formulas.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.teaches: Recall: definitions, the table, the multiplication rule.
stages.interaction: Q.drill prompt: 'Interviewer: what availability would you target here, and what does it mean in practice?' Model answer: 'I'd target three to four nines. 99.9% allows about 43 minutes of downtime a month, 8.8 hours a year; 99.99% allows about 4.4 minutes a month, 53 minutes a year. Every nine is ten times less downtime and usually a lot more cost. Our availability can't beat the product of our hard dependencies, three 99.9% services in a row give about 99.7%, so I'd add redundancy where it counts and keep the failures independent, for example replicas in different zones. Internally I'd set an SLO a bit tighter than any SLA we sign.'
stages.check: Self-grade checks: 'Converted a percentage to downtime (e.g. 99.9% ≈ 43 min/month)', 'Said each nine = 10× less downtime', 'Mentioned that chained dependencies multiply', 'Mentioned redundancy with independent failures (or SLO vs SLA)'.

caveats: Table 2-3 uses a 365.25-day year; with 365 days the yearly numbers shift by about 0.07% (e.g. 8.76 vs 8.77 hours). Irrelevant in an interview.
Series/parallel math, SLO/SLI and error budgets are not in the book chapter; they come from the Google SRE book and are common senior-level follow-ups.
Redundancy math assumes independent failures. Real outages are often correlated (shared region, power, config push, bad deploy), so real availability is lower than the formula says.
A provider SLA is a contract with service credits, not a promise that the service will be up; specific SLA percentages differ by product and change over time.
